questions.prompt: The probability that a certain free-throw shooter makes a shot is 0.75. What does this mean?
questions.answer: In the long run, over many, many shots, the shooter makes about 75% of them.
solutionSteps: A probability describes what happens over many repetitions, not in a few shots.
Probability is long-run relative frequency; it says nothing exact about short runs.
“Exactly 3 of every 4” and “makes the next three” claim short-run certainty, which probability never gives.

questions.prompt: A coin is tossed 10 times, then 50 times, then 100 times with an applet. What does the law of large numbers predict?
questions.answer: The proportion of heads tends to get closer to 0.5 as the number of tosses increases.
solutionSteps: The law of large numbers is about the proportion of heads, not the count.
As the number of trials grows, the observed proportion settles near the true probability, but short-run results vary.
Heads never becomes “due,” and the proportion need not be exactly 0.5 at any fixed number of tosses.

questions.answer: Let digits 0–6 represent a make and 7–9 a miss; read one random digit per shot.

questions.prompt: A simulation of 200 trials estimated P(at least one 6 in four rolls of a die) as 0.535. What is the best way to make the estimate more accurate?
questions.answer: Run many more trials of the simulation.
solutionSteps: A simulated proportion varies by chance; its accuracy depends on the number of trials.
By the law of large numbers, more repetitions make the simulated proportion closer to the true probability (here 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518).
Rounding, changing the die or reusing the same digits does not get closer to the true value.

questions.prompt: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.45. What is P(A and B)?
solutionSteps: For disjoint events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) and P(A and B) = 0.
Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events cannot occur together, so P(A and B) = 0.

questions.prompt: Free response (Probability: Long-Run Relative Frequency and the Law of Large Numbers). Sam makes 75% of free throws in the long run. In one practice, Sam shoots 20 free throws and makes 12.
questions.answer: (a) 0.6; (b) No: short runs vary a lot; the long-run rate is about the many-trial proportion; (c) 150; (d) No: shots are independent; the probability is still about 0.75; the law of large numbers is about the long run, not correcting short runs

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the relative frequency of made shots in this practice.

parts.label: b

parts.answer: No: short runs vary a lot; the long-run rate is about the many-trial proportion

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: After missing 3 in a row, Sam says, "I’m due to make the next one." Is this reasoning correct? Explain using the law of large numbers.
parts.answer: No: shots are independent; the probability is still about 0.75; the law of large numbers is about the long run, not correcting short runs

solutionSteps: (a) Scoring, 1 point: Correct value.
(b) With only 20 shots, the proportion can easily differ from 0.75 by chance; the long-run rate describes many shots.
(b) Scoring, 1 point: Short-run variability.
(c) Scoring, 1 point: Correct expected count.
(d) Each shot still has probability about 0.75. The law of large numbers says the proportion approaches 0.75 over many shots because the early results are swamped, not because misses are made up.
(d) Scoring, 1 point: Rejects the "due" reasoning with independence and the long-run meaning.
Total: 4 points.
